# Stretching the limits: The challenges and opportunities shaping global pizza cheese production


04 September 2026 in:


[Bioscience](https://www.iff.com/category/bioscience/)[Food & Beverage](https://www.iff.com/category/food-beverage/)


Every pizza lover notices the cheese. The stretch, the melt, the browning, the flavor and the visual appeal all shape the eating experience. But for manufacturers, delivering those qualities consistently has never been more challenging. As consumer expectations evolve and economic pressures intensify, pizza cheese producers around the world are searching for new ways to balance performance, efficiency and profitability.


In this blog, experts from **five key regions** share the challenges shaping their markets – and where the biggest opportunities for innovation lie.


Table of Contents


Toggle


##


**Where Consumer Expectations Meet Cheese Manufacturing**


Pizza may be one of the world’s most familiar foods, but producing the cheese that sits at its heart has become an increasingly sophisticated undertaking.


Consumers expect pizza cheese to deliver every time.


They want the stretch when a slice is lifted. A satisfying melt across the surface is equally important. The right amount of browning and a flavor profile that complements the toppings without overpowering them are also key expectations.


For manufacturers, however, delivering that experience consistently requires navigating an increasingly complex set of variables.


Rising milk costs, labor shortages, sustainability expectations, supply chain pressures and intense competition are forcing producers to find new ways to improve efficiency without compromising quality.


At the same time, consumers are demanding more from the products they buy. Across the dairy sector, trends such as high-protein nutrition, premium experiences, convenience and clean-label products are reshaping expectations.


Pizza cheese sits at the intersection of all these demands.


Yet, the industry’s biggest opportunity may be its ability to respond. Advances in[cultures, enzymes, coagulants and fermentation technologies](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/) are giving manufacturers greater control over cheese functionality than ever before. Producers can increasingly fine-tune meltability, stretch, browning, flavor development, acidification rates and shelf life while improving production efficiency. In many cases, the conversation has shifted from simply making cheese to engineering performance.


That shift is creating new opportunities around the world. While the challenges facing manufacturers may be broadly similar, the solutions being prioritized often reflect the realities of individual markets.


****


##


**Australia and New Zealand: Turning export complexity into competitive advantage**


Australia and New Zealand have built strong reputations as[dairy](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/) exporters, supplying pizza cheese into diverse markets throughout Asia-Pacific and beyond. That global reach creates both challenges and opportunities.


According to Mike Cains, IFF’s regional technical sales manager for cheese cultures and enzymes, the biggest challenge is variability in customer expectations.


Different markets often require different performance characteristics. These can include optimal browning, longer stretch or specific melting properties.


“Everybody wants stretch. Everybody wants melt. But exactly how much stretch, how much browning and how much melt can vary quite significantly depending on where the product is going,” he explains.
For manufacturers, the opportunity lies in creating products that can be tailored to varying market requirements.


At the same time, they need to avoid adding unnecessary complexity to production.


Increasingly, producers are turning to culture and process innovations.


These innovations allow them to fine-tune functionality while maintaining consistency.


They also help manufacturers preserve production efficiency.IFF helps cheese manufacturers create market-specific performance profiles by[combining cultures, coagulants,](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/) application expertise and market insights into tailored solutions that deliver the right functionality, quality, yield and sustainability outcomes for each target market, particularly in export-focused businesses.


##


**Europe: Finding new value in every liter of milk**


Logistics creates another challenge. Much of the region’s pizza cheese is transported long distances. It may also undergo freezing and thawing before reaching consumers.


“You’re not just making a cheese that performs today,” says Cains. “You’re making a cheese that has to perform weeks or months later.”


This has driven greater focus on functionality throughout shelf life. Manufacturers are increasingly looking beyond simple production metrics. They are considering performance across the entire value chain.


As a result, solutions that allow manufacturers to tailor cheese functionality are becoming increasingly important. For example, these solutions can precisely manage proteolysis. This enables the creation of market-specific performance profiles that remain consistent throughout transport, storage and end use.


At the same time, yield optimization remains a major opportunity. Small improvements in moisture retention and process efficiency can generate significant financial returns at scale. The industry’s focus is increasingly shifting towards achieving those gains without sacrificing the sensory qualities that customers value.


###


Improving yield through culture innovation


This is where culture selection is becoming an increasingly valuable commercial lever. Cains points to a recent example where a pizza cheese producer switched from its existing starter culture to IFF’s[CHOOZIT®](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/choozit/) mozzarella cultures. Rather than requiring a major process overhaul, the transition involved only a minor recipe adjustment to improve moisture stability. Because our mozzarella cultures acidify quickly while remaining highly tolerant of normal production variability, the cheesemaker gained greater process control and more consistent performance without disrupting operations. Once the process had been fine-tuned, the manufacturer achieved significant improvement in cheese yield. At industrial production volumes, that represents a significant improvement in profitability while maintaining the functionality customers expect.


In Europe, one of the biggest opportunities for manufacturers lies in improving yield while preserving product quality. As milk costs remain under pressure, producers are looking for ways to maximize output from every liter processed. One approach involves increasing moisture retention within mozzarella and pizza cheese products, effectively generating more saleable product from the same milk volume.


However, the challenge is ensuring that increased moisture does not negatively affect functionality. “The cheesemaker wants to produce a higher-moisture mozzarella without any negative impact on shelf life,” says IFF’s cheese application specialist for Europe, Mikael Pianfetti.


“Through significant investments in research and innovation, IFF is developing solutions that help cheesemakers optimize performance and yield, enhance efficiency and maintain the quality consumers expect” Pianfetti notes.


Culture solutions such as IFF’s[CHOOZIT®](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/choozit/) range are designed to help producers fine-tune acidification, meltability and browning characteristics while supporting consistent functionality throughout shelf life. Rather than relying on formulation changes alone, producers are increasingly using culture selection as a lever for both quality and efficiency.


Europe’s label-friendly* environment is also accelerating innovation.


Rather than relying on additives, many manufacturers are looking to solutions that achieve functionality naturally.


These solutions use cultures, enzymes and fermentation to deliver the desired cheese performance. At the same time, producers are exploring opportunities to differentiate through flavor.


“When you eat a pizza, traditionally it’s the other toppings that drive the flavor experience.


But some customers are beginning to ask us for higher flavor, buttery flavor in pizza cheese.” This growing interest in flavor development represents a new frontier for the category. Historically, pizza cheese has focused primarily on texture and functionality.


India’s pizza market continues to expand rapidly, creating enormous opportunities for[da](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/)[i](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/)[ry](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/) manufacturers. Driven by urbanization, changing lifestyles and the growth of quick-service restaurant chains, demand for pizza cheese continues to increase across the country. For producers, the challenge is no longer simply meeting demand but doing so efficiently and consistently. “The market is growing quickly, and producers need solutions that allow them to scale while maintaining consistency,” says Dnyaneshwar Chavan, IFF’s senior application specialist in the region.


It is a requirement that is accelerating investment in automation, process optimization and manufacturing technologies. These investments help improve repeatability and consistency in production.


One particularly important area of opportunity is reducing the time required to achieve optimal cheese functionality. Traditionally, mozzarella production involves days of ripening before the desired performance characteristics emerge. Reducing ripening times can improve throughput.


It can also reduce inventory requirements. In addition, it allows manufacturers to respond more quickly to customer demand. In a high-growth market, these gains can deliver substantial commercial advantages.


##


**India: Meeting explosive demand without compromising quality**


Helping manufacturers achieve these gains requires improvements across several stages of the cheesemaking process. Fast-acidifying starter cultures, such as IFF’s[CHOOZIT®](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/choozit/) FIT range, delivered in freeze-dried format, allow producers to shorten acidification times while delivering reliable processing and the melt and stretch properties required for pizza applications.


“The robustness of the range also helps manufacturers maintain consistent cheese quality despite the seasonal variations in milk composition commonly experienced across India, which can naturally impact cheesemaking performance and yield” Chavan notes.


To further support culture performance and reliability, IFF works closely with cheesemakers through tailored phage management services.


The company also provides sample analysis through its dedicated Phage Technical Service. These services help identify risks early. They also help maintain culture performance over time.


Coagulants such as CHYMOSTAR® and[MARZYME™](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/marzyme/) help optimize coagulation while providing better control over proteolysis, contributing to improved texture and meltability. Meanwhile, adjunct cultures can help manufacturers manage browning characteristics, giving producers greater flexibility to tailor finished products for different market requirements.
****


##


**Latin America: Balancing affordability and indulgence**


The opportunity is considerable. In Brazil alone, mozzarella production increased by 66% between 2022 and 2024,\[1\] , while around 90% of pizza launches across Latin America last year featured cheese as a flavor or ingredient.\[2\]


In this region, pizza remains closely associated with enjoyment, convenience and social connection. “Usually when you go out for a pizza, or bake some pizza at home, you go together with friends and family; it’s a moment of relaxation,” says Antonio Salles, IFF’s principal application specialist for dairy. That consumer mindset creates a different innovation agenda.


While health and wellness trends continue to influence broader food markets, pizza cheese manufacturers in the region are largely focused on preserving the sensory experience consumers love. At the same time, they are looking for ways to improve operational performance.


The opportunity lies in delivering better economics without compromising indulgence. Yield optimization remains a major priority as producers look for ways to maximize profitability. However, unlike some markets, manufacturers must often balance moisture retention targets with the requirements of sliced cheese applications, which remain particularly important across parts of Latin America.


As production volumes increase, maintaining reliable fermentation becomes increasingly important. Phage management has therefore become a growing area of focus. Drawing on one of the world’s largest collections of dairy bacteriophages, gathered from production facilities across multiple regions. IFF continuously evaluates the resistance of its cultures and proactively strengthens them before phage susceptibility becomes apparent in commercial production.


Rather than relying on standard rotation programs, IFF develops tailored phage management strategies for individual cheesemakers, designing intelligent culture rotations that reflect each customer’s manufacturing processes and operating environment. The result is more robust fermentations, reduced production risk and greater operational consistency.
****


##


**North America: Reducing variability, increasing performance**


North America remains one of the world’s leading pizza cheese markets. Mozzarella now accounts for around 18.5% of all cheese consumed in the United States by volume, with demand growing by a further 2.3% over the past year.\[3\] That growth continues to place pressure on manufacturers to deliver greater consistency, higher throughput and predictable functionality at industrial scale.


For James Musetti, IFF’s senior application scientist, the defining challenge remains consistency. “It’s about delivering predictable functionality at scale,” he says. “Having a predictable performance and a predictable window of when the cheese will be used – and even trying to extend that window as long as they can.”


Process consistency begins with reliable acidification. Culture systems such as[CHOOZIT®](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/choozit/) SWIFT are designed to deliver predictable acidification profiles, reducing variability in moisture, texture and functionality across high-throughput production environments. Alongside[culture](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) design, IFF works with manufacturers on tailored phage management programs that combine diagnostics, culture rotation strategies and operational best practices to reduce production risk and minimize costly downtime.


Asked to describe the perfect pizza cheese, Musetti points to a combination of sensory and functional attributes.


> “The cheese melts. It has a good stretch on the pizza. It doesn’t stretch too long, but it doesn’t break too easily,” he says.
>
>
> “Visually, it needs to be appealing. It should have small, tiny blisters that are evenly browned with a nice light background.”


Delivering these attributes consistently while improving efficiency is where many manufacturers see their greatest opportunity.


> “There is always pressure to get more cheese per vat and improve productivity. The challenge is doing that without negatively impacting functionality.”


Functionality must also be maintained throughout shelf life. By combining carefully selected cultures with coagulants such as CHYMOSTAR® and[MARZYME®](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/marzyme/) , manufacturers can optimize curd formation, maximize yield and deliver the melt, stretch and browning characteristics customers expect, even as products age. For brands seeking greater product differentiation, adjunct cultures and lipases also allow flavor profiles to be tailored from mild to more pronounced cheese notes without compromising pizza performance.


Collectively, these improvements translate into higher throughput, fewer downgrades and lower manufacturing costs – benefits that are becoming increasingly valuable as competition intensifies.
****
**Engineering the future of pizza cheese**
****
The challenges facing pizza cheese manufacturers are significant, but so are the opportunities.


Across all regions, producers are responding to market pressures with new approaches to cultures, fermentation, functionality management, yield and process optimization. While priorities differ from region to region, the direction of travel is remarkably similar.


The industry is moving beyond simply producing cheese and towards engineering performance.


Whether the goal is increasing yield, improving shelf life, reducing production risk, accelerating ripening times or creating new flavor experiences, innovation is giving manufacturers more tools than ever before to achieve their objectives.


> For pizza cheese producers, the future will not be defined solely by the challenges they face. It will be shaped by how effectively they turn those challenges into opportunities.


*The term ‘label-friendly’ refers to products that enable a simpler
label with fewer and recognizable ingredients for consumers.
